headline: Uganda's Tree-Planting Push Protects Mountain Gorillas
meta_description: Communities near Bwindi National Park plant trees to reduce pressure on gorilla habitats, letting residents meet their needs without entering the forest.
summary_short: Ugandan communities are planting trees near Bwindi Impenetrable National Park to keep residents from harvesting inside the forest, protecting the habitat of nearly half…
body:
Communities living near Bwindi Impenetrable National Park in Uganda have launched a clever conservation effort: planting useful trees along the forest's edge so residents can harvest medicine, firewood, and timber without venturing into gorilla territory. The strategy addresses a real tension—the park's population of mountain gorillas, around 450 individuals, continues to grow, but the forest itself cannot expand. By providing accessible resources outside the park, neighbors have less incentive to cut trees within it. "Being a neighbor to the park, I understand that the number of gorillas is increasing, but the forest habitat is not increasing," explained Christina Katushabe, founder of Change a Life Bwindi, the organization driving the effort. The work matters because mountain gorillas were once critically endangered. A 2018 survey found the global population above 1,000—a remarkable recovery that now classifies them as merely endangered rather than critically endangered.

The Uganda Wildlife Authority distributes seedlings selected by members of the Batwa, an Indigenous community whose knowledge shapes which species get planted. Tourism has supported gorilla recovery by creating jobs and revenue for nearby communities, and the tree-planting campaign extends these benefits by offering alternative livelihoods. Women's crafts groups sell locally made goods to visitors, while students at schools like Ruhijja Seed Secondary School participate in tree planting, learning conservation firsthand. "Now we are going to protect the forest, so that our gorillas can stay well," said one student, Davis Musinguzi.

What emerges from this work is something deeper than a simple resource-sharing arrangement. As one crafts group member, Eunice Owembabazi, put it: "we people and the gorillas do not inconvenience each other." The trees create space for coexistence, turning neighbors into guardians of the same forest.
quick_facts: 450 mountain gorillas live in Bwindi Impenetrable National Park—nearly half the world's population
Communities plant medicinal trees, timber, and firewood sources outside the park boundary
Uganda Wildlife Authority and Change a Life Bwindi lead the tree-planting initiative
Global mountain gorilla population recovered from critically endangered to endangered status
Indigenous Batwa community selects tree species based on medicinal and practical uses
